title: 2 Samuel 23:1–7
context: David’s last words describe him as the anointed of the God of Jacob through whom the LORD’s Spirit spoke, and they picture a ruler who governs righteously in the fear of God as morning light after rain. David rests on the everlasting covenant God made with his house, while the ungodly are like thorns to be burned. Both traditions read this as shared ground on God’s covenant faithfulness to David, and many Christians in both see the righteous ruler fulfilled in Christ, as a reading.

verses.text: Now these are the last words of David. David the son of Jesse says, the man who was raised on high says, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel:
verses.arminianNotes:
The passage is introduced as “the last words of David,” with David described as raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel. Arminian readers note the humble origin behind the titles: “the son of Jesse” who was raised up by God.

The phrase likely refers to his final poetic testimony rather than literally his final utterance (cf. 1 Kings 2:1–9).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see David’s titles as gifts of God’s grace: he was raised up, anointed, and given songs for Israel.

The title “anointed” links David with the covenant line that Christians see culminating in the Messiah, which is a reading that both traditions share.

verses.text: “The LORD’s Spirit spoke by me. His word was on my tongue.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s Spirit spoke by me. His word was on my tongue.” Arminian readers note that David claims divine inspiration for his words, a claim the New Testament affirms (Matt 22:43; Acts 2:30).

God’s word comes through a human speaker without erasing his voice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a clear statement of inspiration, consistent with 2 Peter 1:21.

The verse is often cited in both traditions in discussions of Scripture’s divine and human authorship.

verses.text: The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me, ‘One who rules over men righteously, who rules in the fear of God,
verses.arminianNotes:
The Rock of Israel speaks of “One who rules over men righteously, who rules in the fear of God.” Arminian readers note that the ideal ruler is defined by righteousness and reverence, not power alone.

The standard judges every king, including David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the portrait of a righteous king that David himself did not fully embody.

Many Christians read the description as pointing to Christ, the righteous king (cf. Isa 11:1–5), which is a reading held in both traditions.

verses.text: shall be as the light of the morning when the sun rises, a morning without clouds, when the tender grass springs out of the earth, through clear shining after rain.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Such a ruler is like morning light, a cloudless dawn, and grass springing up after rain. Arminian readers note the images of blessing and renewal that just rule brings to a people.

Good government is pictured as life-giving (cf. Ps 72:6).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see creation imagery describing the blessing of righteous rule.

The picture of light after rain suggests hope and restoration, which Christians often connect with the reign of Christ, as a reading.

verses.text: Isn’t my house so with God? Yet he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure, for it is all my salvation and all my desire. Won’t he make it grow?
verses.arminianNotes:
“Isn’t my house so with God? Yet he has made with me an everlasting covenant, ordered in all things, and sure.” Arminian readers note David’s confidence in God’s covenant (2 Sam 7:12–16).

The Hebrew of the first line can be read as a question or a statement, and translations differ.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the covenant as David’s whole salvation and desire, resting on God’s faithfulness rather than David’s record (cf. Ps 89:3–4; Isa 55:3).

Both traditions treat God’s covenant promise as shared ground, while noting that the opening line is ambiguous in Hebrew.

verses.text: But all the ungodly will be as thorns to be thrust away, because they can’t be taken with the hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But all the ungodly will be as thorns to be thrust away.” Arminian readers note the contrast between the righteous ruler and the ungodly, who cannot be handled safely.

The image warns of the danger of wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the judgment that falls on the ungodly as the counterpart to covenant blessing.

The thorn image depicts wickedness as harmful to those who touch it.

verses.text: The man who touches them must be armed with iron and the staff of a spear. They will be utterly burned with fire in their place.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The man who handles thorns must be armed with iron and spear, and the thorns will be burned. Arminian readers note the final judgment on the ungodly pictured as fire.

The poem ends soberly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see judgment pictured in fire.

The poem closes with both covenant hope and warning, a pattern both traditions recognize throughout Scripture.
